I am getting old now, and with only two people at home, I cannot spread myself too thin. So this year I will still do what I know best. Most of the land I keep in wheat-maize, because that is the steady way here. Cotton I still plant on part of the land, but not too much, because cotton needs more hand work and picking. I do not read books, I farm by what I have seen on my own fields. If wheat is too thin, I lose grain. If maize misses the rain after wheat harvest, it suffers fast. If cotton gets too much land, the picking tires us out. So I keep the plan balanced: enough wheat and maize for stable income, some cotton for cash, but not so much that the two of us cannot handle it.

For wheat, I sow in early October on the better fields, about the same time as everybody else. I use the seed I know from the local dealer, not the fancy expensive one. I put base fertilizer before sowing, then topdress once when the wheat starts taking off in spring. If the winter and spring stay dry, I will irrigate three times, mainly before winter, at jointing, and around grain filling if needed. For maize, after wheat harvest I do not waste time. The turnaround is too tight, so I clear the field quick, do shallow tillage or direct planting if I can hire the machine in time, and sow within a few days. Maize gets one base dose and one topdress when it grows fast. Cotton I keep on a smaller piece. Cotton brings cash if the year is decent, but it needs more watching and more labor, so I do not expand it. I fertilize it in a simple way, one base and one topdress, and irrigate only when the soil is really dry because pumping water costs money.
